name: Treaty with the Cherokee, 1785 (Treaty of Hopewell)
promises: Article 4 fixed the boundary of the lands allotted to the Cherokees for their hunting grounds.

Article 5: any United States citizen who settled on those lands, or did not leave within six months of ratification, would forfeit the protection of the United States, and the Cherokees could punish him as they pleased.
Article 9: the United States alone would regulate trade with the Cherokees.
Article 12: the Cherokees could send a deputy of their choice to Congress whenever they thought fit.

breaches.what: The Supreme Court held that Georgia's law extending its jurisdiction over Cherokee territory was void as repugnant to the treaties of Hopewell and Holston, and that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct community in which Georgia's laws had no force.

source.title: Worcester v. Georgia, 31 U.S. 515 (1832)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School

breaches.what: The National Park Service states that Georgia ignored the Worcester ruling and the federal judicial and executive branches did nothing to enforce it.
breaches.whoFoundIt: National Park Service, Fort Smith National Historic Site

source.title: Cherokee Relations with US Government Before Removal

landTaken: The hunting grounds bounded by Article 4 east of the Mississippi were ceded by later treaties, finally by the Treaty of New Echota (1835); see kappler-447.
compensation: None located for the breaches recorded here.
today: Not researched beyond the removal; see the Treaty of New Echota (kappler-447).

nationVoice.summary: The Nation's history describes the removal forced on it after the 1835 treaty.

openQuestions: Kappler gives no ratification or proclamation date for this treaty, made under the Articles of Confederation; none is recorded here.
Settlement on Cherokee lands inside the Article 4 boundary in the years after 1785 (North Carolina and the State of Franklin) is described by historians; no formal finding was opened.
Worcester v. Georgia found that Georgia, a state, acted against the treaty; the federal failure to enforce rests on the National Park Service's statement, not on a ruling.
